summary: An alphabetic hymn of daily praise to God the King: unsearchably great, gracious and merciful, near to all who call.

context.title: An alphabet of praise
paragraphs: Psalm 145 is an acrostic: its verses begin with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order. [c1] The line for nun is missing from the Hebrew after verse 13; the Septuagint and other ancient versions supply one, modelled on verse 17, and one Hebrew manuscript has it, though Ellicott doubts it there. [c2] Gill reports a Talmudic explanation from Rashi: nun opens Amos’s lament over fallen Israel. [c3]

Its heading names it a tehillah of David, a song of praise, and from its first verse addresses God as King. [c4] In Jewish prayer it is the heart of the Ashre, said twice in the morning service and once in the afternoon. [c5] The Talmud promises a share in the world to come to whoever recites it three times a day. [c6]

Verse 8 takes up the Lord’s description of himself to Moses in Exodus 34:6, almost word for word. [c7] Verse 9 widens that mercy: the LORD is good to all, and his compassion reaches all his works, not Israel alone. [c8] The verses chosen for today end by bringing this greatness near to everyone who calls on him in truth. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: Hebrew says there is “no searching” of God’s greatness: no inquiry ever reaches its bottom.
translationNotes.body: Ḥeqer is a searching out, and with ein it says that something cannot be searched. [c10] Keil and Delitzsch explain that God’s greatness is so deep that no searching can reach its bottom. [c11] Isaiah 40:28 uses the same phrase for God’s understanding, and the Cambridge Bible hears that verse echoed here. [c12] Today’s first reading makes a similar point about God’s plans and paths. [c13]

translationNotes.summary: Two adjectives used almost only of God, taken from Exodus 34:6 with their order reversed, as in several later books.
translationNotes.body: Both adjectives are used in the Bible almost only of God, though Psalm 112:4 may apply them to the upright. [c14] Exodus 34:6 has the older order, raḥum veḥannun; Psalm 145:8 reverses it, as do Joel, Jonah and Nehemiah. [c15] In Jonah 4:2 the prophet names this very pair to explain why he fled towards Tarshish. [c16] Jewish fast-day services read the Exodus passage aloud, with its thirteen qualities of mercy. [c17]

translationNotes.summary: Ḥasid, often “holy” in English, comes from ḥesed, kindness; said of God it means loving, full of kindness.
translationNotes.body: Ḥasid belongs with ḥesed, kindness, and BDB favours an active sense: one who shows kindness. [c18] The Septuagint rendered it hosios, holy. [c19] Applied to God it occurs only here and in Jeremiah 3:12, where the Cambridge Bible takes it as full of lovingkindness. [c20] The line pairs it with the LORD being righteous in all his ways. [c21]

translationNotes.summary: Qarov, near, is the word Isaiah 55:6 also uses: the God beyond searching is close to those who call.
translationNotes.body: Qarov is the ordinary adjective for near, used of cities, roads and neighbours. [c22] Isaiah 55:6, today’s first reading, uses it of God: he is to be called on while he is near. [c23] The psalm adds a condition, calling on him in truth, which the Pulpit Commentary reads as sincerity rather than mere formal prayer. [c24] The same psalm that calls his greatness unsearchable calls him near. [c25]

claims.text: Psalm 145 is written alphabetically, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

The nun verse is missing from the Hebrew after Psalm 145:13; the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac and other versions supply a verse there, a variation of Psalm 145:17; Ellicott adds that it is found in one Hebrew manuscript, though he thinks it suspicious there.
Gill reports that Jarchi (Rashi) gives a reason from the Talmud for the missing nun: the prophecy of Israel’s fall in Amos 5:2 begins with that letter.
Psalm 145:1 is headed תְּהִלָּה לְדָוִד, the noun meaning praise or song of praise, and the psalm addresses God as the King.
In Jewish prayer Psalm 145, prefixed by the Ashre verses, is recited twice in the morning and once in the afternoon prayer.
The Talmud (Berakhot 4b) says that whoever recites Psalm 145 three times a day may be certain of a portion in the world to come.
Psalm 145:8 is taken almost verbatim from Exodus 34:6.
Psalm 145:9 says the LORD is good to all and his compassion is over all his works, which commentators take to mean all mankind and all creation, not Israel alone.
Psalm 145:18 says the LORD is near to all who call on him in truth.
The Hebrew noun חֵקֶר means searching or a thing to be searched out, and אֵין חֵקֶר means it is unsearchable (Psalm 145:3; Isaiah 40:28).
Keil and Delitzsch explain that God’s greatness is so deep that no searching can reach its bottom.
Isaiah 40:28 uses אֵין חֵקֶר of God’s understanding, and the Cambridge Bible lists Isaiah 40:28 among the passages Psalm 145:3 echoes.
Isaiah 55:8-9, the first reading of the same Sunday, says God’s thoughts and ways are higher than human thoughts and ways.
BDB describes the adjectives חַנּוּן (gracious) and רַחוּם (compassionate) as used only of God, but its list includes Psalm 112:4, where the pair follows a mention of the upright.
Exodus 34:6 has the earlier order רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן; Psalm 145:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2 and Nehemiah 9:17 have the later order חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם.
In Jonah 4:2 Jonah names God as gracious and compassionate when explaining why he fled to Tarshish.
On Jewish fast-days the Torah lesson from Exodus (32:11-14; 34:1-10), which treats the thirteen qualities of mercy, is read publicly.
BDB defines חָסִיד as kind, pious, and favours an active sense: one who practises חֶסֶד, kindness.
The Septuagint renders חָסִיד in Psalm 145:17 as ὅσιος, holy.
Applied to God, חָסִיד occurs only in Psalm 145:17 and Jeremiah 3:12, and means full of lovingkindness.
Psalm 145:17 pairs the LORD being righteous in all his ways with being חָסִיד in all his works.
קָרוֹב is the ordinary Hebrew adjective near, used of cities, roads and persons such as neighbours.
Isaiah 55:6 uses קָרוֹב of God: he is to be called on while he is near.
Psalm 145:18 limits God’s nearness to those who call on him in truth, which the Pulpit Commentary explains as sincerely, since mere formal prayer is useless.
Psalm 145 calls God’s greatness unsearchable (145:3) and says he is near to all who call on him (145:18).
